agent_notes: The superscription is verse 1 in the Hebrew (KJV 108:0, no number), so every KJV verse number in this psalm is one lower than the Hebrew's. I translated each Hebrew verse as it stands.

Rashi reads 'cast my sandal over Edom' as servants taking off the speaker's sandals; the other common reading is a gesture of taking possession. The text does not say which, so the literal layer stays literal and the commentary names both. I could not source the possession reading in the packet's commentaries, so the note on it has no source.

הלא at the head of the verse can be a question ('have you not rejected us?') or, as in the ASV, a statement leading into 'and you do not go out'. I kept the question in the literal layer, which is how most of the five versions take the first half. The second half is a plain statement in all of them.

Revised after the request: the dramatic layer has no vocative, no 'Give it now' and no 'leaned on it long enough'. Urgency comes from the bare imperative and the flat verdict on human rescue. 'mitsar' is taken as 'from the foe' (STEPBible, ASV), though the same consonants can be the noun 'distress', which is how the KJV reads it; the commentary says so.

agent_notes: בֵּאלֹהִים: STEPBible reads 'in God' with the preposition בְּ. The English versions split between 'through God' (KJV, ASV, Webster), 'in God' (YLT) and 'with God' (BBE). The literal layer keeps 'in God'; the dramatic layer uses 'with' because that is how a hearer would take the instrumental/accompanying sense.
Metzudat Zion cites Isaiah 14:19 ('כפגר מובס') for יָבוּס. I take the citation from the packet as given and did not check the verse myself.

agent_notes: כבודי 'my glory': rendered 'my glory' in the literal layer and 'my very soul' in the dramatic one, following Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion, who take it as the soul/self. Ibn Ezra's parallel with 'my heart rejoices and my glory exults' supports it. Rashi's second reading ('even in keeping with my honor') is a different sense.

The remark in the commentary that Shachar is also the name of a Canaanite dawn deity is my own reading and unsourced here; I flagged it as such in the text. The KJV does not play on the root עור either, so this is an audit point, not a claim that the psalmist is polemicizing.

agent_notes: STEPBible marks בָּלְאֻמִּים with (V), a variant reading; I glossed the form as it stands. Radak notes the lamed is soft where a dagesh would be expected; no effect on the meaning.

agent_notes: מחקקי: STEPBible has 'commander's staff', the KJV 'lawgiver', the ASV 'sceptre'. The participle of חקק means one who engraves or decrees, and a cognate noun (מחקק) is a ruler's staff elsewhere. I kept 'my lawgiver' in the literal layer and offered 'staff' in the commentary. The Hebrew is the same as in Ps 60, so the split between the English versions is old.

Нумерация: в еврейском тексте надписание — стих 1, в Синодальной Библии это Пс 107:1 без отдельного номера у надписания (там Пс 107 соответствует ивритскому Пс 108, а стихи сдвинуты на один). Номера стихов в корпусе — еврейские.
Edom передан как «Едом» (а не «Идумея» Синодальной), чтобы имя совпадало с ивритским и с комментарием; Синодальная читает «Идумея» — упомянул в комментарии к ст. 11.
